$comment: Pinned toolchain for BLACKHEART's Solidity analysis engines. This file is the single source of truth for what `blackheart engines bootstrap` installs and what `blackheart engines doctor` verifies. Versions are pinned exactly: a floating version would make a finding unreproducible in another sandbox. Update a pin only with a note explaining why.

python.$comment: The venvs are built with the interpreter that runs blackheart. Requires >=3.11 (the package floor).

slither.resource_notes: CPU-bound; a 30k-LOC project compiles in tens of seconds. No network needed after install.

wake.resource_notes: Ships its own Solidity front end, so it needs no solc. Static detectors are fast; its fuzzer is slower.

halmos.resource_notes: Symbolic execution needs a Foundry project and a solver (z3 is bundled via its dependency). Memory- and time-heavy: a single test can take minutes and the solver can diverge. Always bounded by --solver-timeout and the adapter's wall clock.

echidna.resource_notes: Native binary, no Python. Needs crytic-compile (from the slither venv) and forge to compile a Foundry target. Fuzzing is CPU-bound; --test-limit bounds the work.

medusa.resource_notes: Native Go binary. Coverage-guided sequence fuzzing is the heaviest engine here: bound testLimit and workers. Needs crytic-compile and forge to compile.

forge.resource_notes: Required by crytic-compile's Foundry platform, which Slither, Echidna and Medusa all use to compile a Foundry target. Without it, compilation raises FileNotFoundError and the engine exits non-zero -- which must never be read as a clean scan.

solc.resource_notes: Installed through solc-select (in the slither venv). A target that pins a different pragma needs that version added; the adapter does not guess a compiler version.

notes: Every engine is installed into its own venv under ~/.blackheart/venvs (or a downloaded binary under ~/.blackheart/bin), never into the system interpreter: slither-analyzer ships a top-level `tests` package that shadows this repository's tests/ directory.
The shared venv path means crytic-compile is available to Echidna and Medusa without a second install.
Nothing here needs a paid service, an API key, or network access after installation.

bytecode_tools are engines that consume EVM bytecode rather than Solidity source (currently heimdall). They are installed and verified by the same manifest machinery but are deliberately kept out of SOLIDITY_ENGINES, so the source-analysis orchestrator never hands them a project they cannot read.

known_incompatibilities: Operates on EVM runtime bytecode only: it takes a deployed address, a hex blob or a .bin file, never a Solidity source tree. It is therefore not part of SOLIDITY_ENGINES and is not driven by the source-analysis orchestrator.
Without --include-sol it writes only abi.json; the decompiled source requires that flag.
Function names are unresolved unless a selector database is reachable, so output carries Unresolved_<selector> placeholders offline.
heimdall.resource_notes: Native Rust binary, ~14 MB, no runtime dependencies. A 2 KB runtime decompiles in a few seconds; large contracts take minutes. The pinned sha256 is a reproducibility pin computed from the official release asset on the verified_on date, not an upstream-signed attestation: it detects a silent re-upload, not a compromised maintainer. The 0.9.3 release tag ships a binary that reports itself as 0.9.2, so version is pinned to what the binary prints, which is what doctor compares.
